title: Military's No. 2 defends GlobalEye surveillance jets despite capability concerns
summary: Canada's second-in-command is standing behind the proposed purchase of six Saab GlobalEye surveillance jets despite air force concerns about their capabilities. Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee told MPs…

image.caption: Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee is seen at a conference in Ottawa in March. He told MPs on Monday that he's satisfied with the program to purchase Saab's GlobalEye. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada's second-in-command is standing behind the proposed purchase of six Saab GlobalEye surveillance jets despite air force concerns about their capabilities. Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee told MPs he's satisfied with the procurement process, arguing the aircraft will contribute to an integrated continental defence network alongside satellites and ground-based radar systems.
Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee tells committee he's satisfied with program
The second in command of the Canadian military told parliamentarians on Monday that he's satisfied with the way the program to buy airborne early warning planes is unfolding.

Vice-Admiral Angus Topshee made the comments in testimony before the House of Commons defence committee, which is studying Bill C-40, legislation intended to turn the Defence Investment Agency (DIA) into a Crown corporation.

Earlier this year, Prime Minister Mark Carney surprised many in the defence community by announcing Canada opened negotiations with Swedish defence giant Saab to purchase six of their GlobalEye surveillance jets — aircraft that would be militarized in Canada based upon a Bombardier 6500 airframe.
The federal government and the company have since agreed on a term sheet, a non-binding document that sets the stage for an eventual contract.

items: Feds sign preliminary deal with Saab for 6 GlobalEye aircraft
Ottawa chose surveillance plane without knowing it met military needs

blocks.text: In early September, multiple sources told CBC News that the air force was concerned the GlobalEye meets only a handful of the military's requirements.

On Monday, federal Conservatives pressed Topshee, the vice-chief of the defence staff, for assurances that military requirements would not be sacrificed for the sake of building up the country's defence industrial base.
"I am comfortable with the path we're proceeding down," Topshee told the three-party committee, referring to the GlobalEye program.

He said the airborne surveillance capability is crucial for the defence of North America and ties into an integrated air and missile defence system with the United States — a program U.S. President Donald Trump has nicknamed the Golden Dome.
Canada chose GlobalEye spy plane without knowing military's needs: sources
Topshee defended the choice of the GlobalEye, saying that NATO also plans to acquire it.
The air force, however, is concerned that the plane, under its current design and configuration, doesn't have 360-degree radar coverage and that blind spots are created during turns.
There are also concerns about the range and frequency of the radar.
Saab has proposed modifications, putting additional radar sets in the nose and tail.

The air force also has concerns about the number of crew stations and connectivity equipment to plug the plane into the NORAD network, which would limit the GlobalEye's ability to offer a "control" function during operations that involve a series of military assets.

blocks.text: The military is also seeking a radar plane that can be refuelled in flight to cover the vast expanses of the Arctic, a feature that is not currently included on the GlobalEye.
"Every platform has advantages and disadvantages," Topshee said.
He also testified that the modern battlespace is changing rapidly with the introduction of drones and autonomous systems.
To maintain surveillance, the military, Topshee said, would rely on not only the GlobalEye, but also ground-based radar and satellites to get "the full picture."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
